meta.name: Sigil Core — Obfuscation Chain Patterns
meta.author: NOMARK <hello@sigilsec.ai>
meta.description: Advanced multi-stage obfuscation: nested Base64 chains, Unicode steganography, dynamic function construction, and import-time side effects. Ported from Python ENHANCED_OBFUSCATION_RULES.

rules.description: Nested Base64 chain decoding — advanced obfuscation technique
rules.remediation: Decode the nested layers yourself and read what comes out. One Base64 layer is all any honest Python (base64.b64decode) or JavaScript (atob) transport needs; a second layer exists only to keep the payload out of text search, so if the decoded result reaches exec, eval, Function, a shell or a socket, reject the package.

rules.description: Base64 decoding with dynamic key construction
rules.remediation: Reconstruct the value being handed to base64.b64decode or atob from its parts and read it. Repairing padding on a JWT or URL-safe segment (segment + padding) is the one common honest shape; a blob assembled from several literals or scattered variables was split so that no single string looks suspicious, and the joined result must be reviewed before install.

rules.description: Mixed Base64 and URL encoding chain
rules.remediation: In Python, unquoting a percent-encoded request parameter and then Base64-decoding it is a normal web-handler shape when the input comes from a request. The reverse order, or a hard-coded literal as the input, means the author encoded their own string twice to hide it — decode it and read the plaintext before deciding.

rules.description: Pickle deserialization with Base64 decoding — dangerous combination
rules.remediation: Python's pickle.loads runs whatever __reduce__ callable the payload names, so a Base64 blob fed straight into it is an arbitrary-code loader. Round-tripping the program's own runtime cache or session data is the only defensible form; a literal blob in the source, or bytes that arrived over the network, is a payload — reject the package.

Run the same two Python decodes (bytes.fromhex, then base64.b64decode) yourself and read the plaintext. No format or protocol needs a Base64 string that is itself hex-encoded; the extra layer only keeps the payload out of grep, so judge the decoded bytes as you would a shell script and reject if they reach exec, subprocess or a socket.

rules.description: Zero-width Unicode characters detected — potential steganography
rules.remediation: Hex-dump the flagged line to see where the zero-width characters sit and what they are hiding. A UTF-8 byte-order mark at the very start of a file, ZWJ inside emoji sequences and ZWNJ in Persian, Arabic or Indic text are legitimate; zero-width characters inside code, identifiers or string literals that are later decoded are steganography or look-alike identifiers, and the file should be rejected.

rules.description: Unicode directional override characters — text direction attack
rules.remediation: Open the file in an editor that shows control characters, or hex-dump the line, and compare what the compiler will parse with what the screen shows. Bidi controls belong only inside user-facing right-to-left strings in localisation files; in code, comments or identifiers they are the Trojan Source technique for making malicious logic read as benign — reject the file.

rules.description: Invisible combining characters detected — potential payload hiding
rules.remediation: Normalise the file to NFC or hex-dump the flagged line to see what the combining marks attach to. Decomposed accents in comments, docs or translation strings are ordinary text; marks stacked on identifiers or on ASCII code, or characters that are later stripped and decoded, are hiding data or forging look-alike names, so read the decoded result before installing.

rules.description: Potential Unicode homograph attack in domain — Cyrillic characters
rules.remediation: Copy the domain out of the flagged line and run it through a punycode converter — an IDN that becomes xn-- is not the ASCII domain it resembles. Russian-language comments or translations that mention a site are harmless; a Cyrillic letter inside a host name the code connects to sends traffic somewhere other than where the reviewer thinks, which is an exfiltration or C2 destination.

rules.description: Dynamic property access with string concatenation or variable reference
rules.remediation: Work out what the bracketed JavaScript expression resolves to. this[name](...) dispatching to a method chosen by a variable is ordinary class and plugin-registry code; window['ev'+'al'] or global[parts joined at runtime] that lands on eval, Function, require, fetch or process is the same call spelled so a text search cannot see it, and the reassembled name decides whether the package is acceptable.

rules.description: Dynamic Function constructor with string building
rules.remediation: new Function over a string built with join or + is JavaScript code generation. Template engines (lodash.template, Handlebars precompile, Vue's runtime compiler) and some bundler runtimes do this deliberately and are recognisable by name; in any other package, print the assembled source and read it, because code built this way never exists as plain text until it runs — reject if it touches the network, the filesystem or child processes.

rules.description: Multiple Unicode escape sequences — potential payload encoding
rules.remediation: Unescape the sequence and see what text it spells. Escaped non-ASCII in JSON, localisation files, regex character classes and minified bundles is routine; a run of \u escapes that spells plain ASCII — an identifier, 'eval', a URL or a shell command — was escaped only to avoid being seen and should be judged as the plain text it decodes to.

rules.description: Mixed script characters in identifiers — potential homograph attack
rules.remediation: Hex-dump the identifiers on the flagged line and check that each is written in a single script. Translation tables and multilingual comments legitimately mix Latin-Extended and Cyrillic text; an identifier that mixes them is a homoglyph — two names that render identically but are different variables or functions — which is the Trojan Source technique for making reviewed code do something other than what it reads as, so reject on any mixed-script identifier.

Convert the JavaScript code points back to text (each number is one character) and read the string. A handful of control or surrogate characters built this way is normal in protocol and polyfill code; a long list that spells 'eval', a URL, 'child_process' or a shell command is a string hidden from text search, and the decoded string decides whether the package is acceptable.

rules.description: Base64 with URL decoding — double encoding obfuscation
rules.remediation: decodeURIComponent(atob(x).split('').map(...).join('')) is the standard browser idiom for reading UTF-8 out of Base64 — JWT payload readers use it everywhere — and is harmless when x is a token or a response. Check what x is: a literal in the source, or a result that then reaches eval, Function, document.write or a script tag, means the double decoding exists to hide the payload, so decode and read it.

rules.description: Python compile+exec with string concatenation — advanced code execution
rules.remediation: Print the concatenated string that Python's compile receives and read it as the program it is. Code generators such as attrs or dataclasses compile a fully-built source held in one variable; two operands joined at the call site are usually a decoded blob plus a trailer or key, meaning the executed code was designed never to appear in plain text — reject unless the generated source is fully visible and benign.

rules.description: Dynamic import with immediate method execution — import-time side effect
rules.remediation: __import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__) and __import__('setuptools').setup(...) are common legacy Python packaging idioms. Anything else called in the same expression — os.system, subprocess.Popen, urllib.request.urlopen, socket.socket, ctypes — is an ordinary import written so 'import os' never appears in the file and runs at import time; judge it by the module and method named and reject if they touch the shell, the network or files outside the package.

rules.description: Dynamic import with encoded module names — import obfuscation
rules.remediation: Decode the module name — the chr() sequence, Base64 blob or fromCharCode call — and see which Python module it resolves to. There is no legitimate reason to encode the name of a module you import; it is done only so that 'os', 'subprocess', 'socket' or 'ctypes' never appear in the source, and the decoded name tells you exactly which capability is being hidden.

rules.description: Python getattr with concatenated attribute names — reflection-based obfuscation
rules.remediation: Join the two quoted fragments and read the Python attribute name they form. A real dynamic getattr takes a variable, not two halves of a literal; splitting the name at the call site exists only to keep 'system', 'Popen', 'urlopen' or 'loads' out of a text search, so treat the joined name as if written plainly and reject if it names a shell, network or deserialisation function.
